Results are noisy so far, so I'm collecting more samples.
Means so far: 0-new-rule task ≈32, 2-new-but-similar ≈27, 3-new-dissimilar ≈37. Checking a trained-task baseline for scale.
Trained task ≈13, 0-new-rule recombination ≈32, 3-new ≈35. Recombination isn't cheap, which points to holistic. Collecting more A vs B samples to confirm.
A (0 new rules, dissimilar) now ≈40 vs B (2 new rules, similar) ≈23, the reverse of what part-based predicts. A few more samples to be sure.

content.text:
I submitted a verdict of **holistic** with confidence 0.85, after using 49 of the 60 budget.

**Design:** I trained the learner on two tasks, L1-S1-M1 and L2-S2-M2. I then picked test tasks where the number of new rules and the similarity to the trained tasks point in opposite directions. I measured similarity with `compare`, the share of inputs on which two tasks give the same response.

| Test task | New rules | Highest similarity to a trained task | Mean examples to criterion |
|---|---|---|---|
| L1-S1-M1 (already trained) | 0 | 1.0 | 13 (n=3) |
| L2-S1-M1 | 0 | 0.06 | 38.4 (n=18) |
| L3-S3-M1 | 2 | 0.625 | 26.0 (n=18) |
| L3-S3-M4 | 3 | 0.06 | 34.9 (n=8) |

**Evidence:**
- **Wrong direction for part-based:** the task with 2 new rules but high similarity was learned faster than the task made entirely of known rules (26 vs 38, z ≈ 2.2). The part-based hypothesis predicts the opposite.
- **New rules made little difference:** the two low-similarity tasks, with 0 and 3 new rules, cost about the same (38 vs 35). Part-based predicts a large gap there.
- **Known rules didn't help:** the task built from known rules cost almost three times as much as the already-trained task.

**Caveats:** single tests are very noisy (one task ranged from 1 to 53), so the main result rests on a moderate gap of about two standard errors. I also used `compare` as a stand-in for the learner's own similarity measure, which can't be observed. That is why the confidence is 0.85 rather than higher.
